C005.subject: class size reduction from 25 to 15 students
C005.object: reading comprehension outcomes for English language learners in grades K-2
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: class size reduction from 25 to 15 students reading comprehension outcomes for English language learners in grades K-2]

[PATH:empirical] Tennessee Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio (STAR) project re-analysis stratified by English language learner status — This large-scale randomized experiment on class size effects in K-3 provides a strong basis to test whether ELL students show differential reading gains at class sizes near 15 versus 25, directly addressing the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal study of dual-language immersion programs with varying class sizes in grades K-2 — Tracking reading comprehension outcomes in programs that naturally vary class size within the 13-17 range compared to 25+ can isolate the effect of size on ELL-specific outcomes, while controlling for instructional approach.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of class size reduction interventions focusing on at-risk and language-minority populations — Synthesizing existing studies that report effect sizes for ELL subgroups can determine whether the hypothesized benefit (and optimal threshold) is consistently observed across contexts, or is confounded by other factors.

C006.subject: class size reduction
C006.object: educational outcomes in early elementary grades
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: class size reduction educational outcomes in early elementary grades]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial (e.g., Project STAR) re-analyzed with instrumental variable methods to isolate class size from teacher quality and resource confounds — Project STAR provides experimental variation in class size; re-analysis using IV or propensity score matching can disentangle selection bias and resource confounding, directly testing the claim that observed effects are spurious.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal administrative data from multiple districts tracking teacher assignment, curriculum changes, and parental involvement alongside class size reductions — By controlling for simultaneous improvements in teacher quality, curricula, and parental programs, this dataset can quantify whether class size reduction retains any independent effect on early elementary outcomes.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of quasi-experimental studies that explicitly adjust for school-level confounders (e.g., fixed effects, difference-in-differences) — A systematic review focusing on studies that address selection bias and resource confounding can synthesize existing evidence to determine whether the correlation vanishes after proper adjustment.

qualifier.mechanism: observed correlations are entirely explained by selection bias and resource confounding
qualifier.evidence: schools implementing class size reduction simultaneously introduce better teachers, curricula, and parental involvement programs

C007.subject: class size reduction combined with peer-assisted learning protocols
C007.object: academic achievement in high school mathematics and science courses
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: class size reduction combined with peer-assisted learning protocols academic achievement in high school mathematics and science courses]

[PATH:empirical] A randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing high school math/science classrooms with reduced class sizes (15-20 students) using structured peer-assisted learning protocols versus standard-size classes with traditional instruction, measuring standardized test scores over two academic years. — An RCT would provide causal evidence on the combined intervention's effect, controlling for confounding variables and directly testing the hypothesis with high internal validity.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on class size reduction and peer-assisted learning in secondary STEM education, focusing on effect sizes and interaction effects. — A meta-analysis can synthesize available evidence to assess whether the combined approach yields moderate-to-large effects, identify heterogeneity across studies, and evaluate the proposed mechanism of increased structured peer interaction.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal observational study tracking student achievement in schools that have implemented the combined intervention, using propensity score matching to compare with similar schools without the intervention. — This design would provide real-world evidence of the intervention's effectiveness in diverse high school settings, addressing external validity and potential implementation challenges, while using matching to reduce selection bias.

qualifier.mechanism: increased opportunities for structured peer interaction

C008.subject: class size reduction
C008.object: improved educational outcomes for older students through increased individualized attention and participation opportunities
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: class size reduction improved educational outcomes for older students through increased individualized attention and participation opportunities]

[PATH:empirical] Tennessee STAR (Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio) project reanalysis focusing on older student cohorts — This large-scale randomized experiment provides longitudinal data that can be re-analyzed to isolate effects of class size reduction on middle and high school outcomes, testing whether structural affordances alone improve participation and attention without pedagogical changes.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of class size effects on secondary education (e.g., Hattie's Visible Learning or the What Works Clearinghouse) — A systematic review of existing studies can quantify the effect size and identify whether the mechanism of increased individualized attention holds for older students, helping to confirm or refute the disputed claim.

[PATH:empirical] Observational study comparing student participation metrics (e.g., question-asking, task engagement) in reduced vs. standard-size secondary classrooms, controlling for teacher practices — Direct measurement of behavioral changes in response to class size reduction, without explicit pedagogical reform, can test the hypothesized structural affordance mechanism and its impact on educational outcomes.

qualifier.mechanism: structural affordances create behavioral changes without explicit pedagogical reform

C011.subject: teacher adaptation frequency in the first semester
C011.object: sustained student achievement gains throughout the academic year independent of initial class size
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: teacher adaptation frequency in the first semester sustained student achievement gains throughout the academic year independent of initial class size]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal classroom observation study tracking weekly instructional adjustments (e.g., differentiated instruction, pacing changes) and linking them to end-of-year standardized test gains, controlling for initial class size, baseline achievement, and SES. — Directly tests the causal claim by measuring adaptation frequency in the first 12 weeks and student achievement over the full year, with class size as a covariate.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of experimental or quasi-experimental studies on teacher professional development programs that emphasize frequent formative assessment and instructional adaptation, examining effect sizes on student achievement across class sizes. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the adaptation-achievement link holds independent of class size, providing statistical power and generalizability.

C012.subject: class size reduction
C012.predicate: produces larger and more replicable gains in
C012.object: educational outcomes than teacher adaptation strategies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: class size reduction educational outcomes than teacher adaptation strategies]

[PATH:empirical] Project STAR (Student Teacher Achievement Ratio) longitudinal data reanalysis with modern causal inference methods — Project STAR is the landmark randomized controlled trial on class size reduction. Reanalyzing its data using current techniques (e.g., instrumental variables, sensitivity analysis) can directly test whether gains from reducing class size below 18 students per class replicate and exceed those from typical teacher adaptation strategies.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of teacher professional development interventions vs. class size reduction RCTs — A systematic meta-analysis comparing effect sizes from high-quality studies of teacher adaptation strategies (e.g., coaching, formative assessment training) with those from class size reduction RCTs would quantify the relative magnitude and replicability of gains, addressing the hypothesis directly.

[PATH:empirical] Cost-effectiveness modeling study using data from multiple school districts implementing both interventions — Empirical cost-effectiveness analysis comparing class size reduction (below 18 students) and teacher adaptation strategies (e.g., targeted PD) in real-world settings can confirm whether the hypothesized larger gains are practically significant when accounting for resource constraints and implementation fidelity.

qualifier.evidence_basis: randomized controlled trials show direct causal mechanisms
